samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both scripts handle consent, the silent observer and the voucher well. A's tasks don't hint at what to click, and its replies stay neutral, with no approval like B's "You're doing great." B gives clearer time limits for stepping in when someone is stuck, but it has the PM unmute to say hello and ask questions, which contradicts the PM's camera and mic staying off, and its photo task names the action. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both handle consent, the observer and the closing well. B's tasks are more neutral (for example, 'Make sure the city can see what it looks like' instead of 'add a photo'), and its replies never praise or approve, while A says 'You're doing great.' A's one edge is a clearer rule for when to step in if someone is stuck, but it also suggests telling participants to type the address first, which hints at the answer.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A's task cards are stronger. They avoid interface words like 'report' and 'add a photo', and A tells the moderator to stay away from those labels. Every reply in A's help table is neutral, while B answers 'Did I do that correctly?' with 'You're doing great', which is approval. B handles the map bug better, with an explicit stuck threshold and a fallback after a second crash, but its close is vaguer about the voucher ('today / within the hour') and asks the PM to speak even though their mic is meant to stay off. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both scripts ask for recording consent before recording starts, say the test is of the form and not the person, introduce the silent PM, and include good tables of neutral replies. B's task cards are more scenario-based and avoid interface wording such as 'report' and 'add a photo to your report'; A's 'You're doing great' reply is slightly evaluative. A is more specific about when to step in (60+ seconds, or a second map break), but B's tighter tasks, think-aloud practice and thorough prep checklist give it a slight edge.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both scripts handle consent, the silent observer and 'test the form, not you' well, and both have good tables of neutral replies. B pulls ahead on stuck participants: it says to step in after about 2 minutes without progress or when the person is visibly frustrated, and gives a graded set of prompts. It also adds a line for when the moderator freezes, which was the user's main worry. A's Task 2 scenario avoids naming the action a little better than B's, but A gives no clear point at which to step in. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both scripts handle consent, the observer, scenario-style tasks and neutral replies well. A is better on the map bug: it pairs the recovery line with a clear rule for when to step in (about 2 minutes with no progress, then a three-step escalation), and it gives the nervous moderator a fallback line for freezing. B handles the bug well but never says when to step in, and it leaves more blanks for the moderator to fill in, such as how Task 3 and the photo step work.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick the same four (#2, #4, #9, #1), rank severity above frequency, and point out that #1 and #9 sit on the same step-1 screen. A is better on rubric item 1 because it says outright that accessibility shouldn't be judged by how often it occurs, while B waves off #5 and #12 as single-session leads. B is better on item 5 because it says six sessions can't predict rates across 30 stores and suggests a retest, though neither answer says glare or reach problems may be more common at other stores, and neither suggests cheap monitoring after rollout. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick the same four fixes (#2, #4, #9, #1), rank failures above friction, and spot that #1 and #9 share a step-1 cause. B frames severity a little better: it argues that accessibility shouldn't be judged by frequency and links the slow help button to the failures it backs up. A, though, is clearer that six sessions can't predict how often problems will occur across 30 stores, and it suggests a cheap retest after the fixes. B's caveat only says the counts are rough, with nothing to watch for after rollout.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick the same four fixes (#2, #4, #9, #1) and rank them by severity, but only A points out that #1 and #9 share a cause and can be fixed with one redesign of the step 1 screen. A also says more clearly how it ranked (by what happened to people, with frequency breaking ties) and notes that the slow help button makes #2 worse. B handles the limits of six sessions better by warning that the single-person failures will recur across 30 stores, but neither answer suggests a cheap way to watch for problems after rollout. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick the same four fixes (#2, #4, #9, #1) and give the same reasons for the ones they left out. B is better because it says it ranked by what happened to people, with frequency only as a tiebreaker, and it notices that #1 and #9 can share one step-1 redesign. A is stronger only on the limits of six sessions: it warns that 1-of-6 failures will recur across 30 stores, but neither answer suggests anything to watch for after rollout.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A ranks by severity more consistently: it picks the unreachable top row (#12), a complete barrier, over the 40-second delay finding the scanner (#1), and it connects related items (#1 with #9, #8 with #4, #13 with #2). Answer B is solid but spends a pick on #1, where nobody failed, and pushes #12 to the roadmap. Neither answer says the issues may be more common at other stores or suggests a cheap check to run after the rollout. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B ranks by severity more consistently. Three of its picks stop people from finishing or lose them items (#2, #4, #12), and it clearly explains why a rare but complete accessibility barrier is worth a pick. A uses half its picks on frequent but recoverable step-1 issues. B also spots more shared causes (#1 with #9, #8 with #4, #13 with #2), but neither answer says glare or accessibility may be more common at other stores or suggests concrete monitoring after rollout.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover close-in reminders with reschedule links, shorter booking windows, evening and weekend slots, and overbooking or a waitlist. Answer A says more about how big the incentive is and suggests gym credit, but it only checks past data and never says to track the no-show rate after the changes. Answer B explicitly tracks show-ups as n of N after the changes, warns about small samples, and suggests asking the people who didn't show what got in the way, which makes it stronger overall. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover close-to-session reminders with easy rescheduling, shorter lead times, better-suited slots, over-booking with a waitlist, and incentive changes that aren't the only fix. A also says to track show-ups as n of N after the changes and suggests asking the no-shows what got in the way, without blaming them. B only analyzes past bookings and never says to measure the no-show rate after the changes, so A wins on the last rubric item.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): The two answers are close and both cover every rubric item. A is slightly ahead on item 5: it explicitly says not to charge no-shows, suggests sending the 7 no-shows a non-judgmental note, lays out a concrete way to check the causes against the existing data, and says to track results as 'n of N'. B adds useful touches (a calendar invite, making the incentive concrete and certain, noting the sampling bias), so its incentive handling is a little stronger. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover all five rubric items well: reminders with reschedule links, shorter lead times with evening and weekend slots, over-booking with a backup list, and an incentive that is not treated as the only fix. B is slightly stronger because it adds a quick check of the existing 7 no-shows against the 8 who came, a non-judgmental follow-up note to the no-shows, more recruiting channels and video-call sessions, and advice to track results as n of N given the small sample. A is a little more specific on tracking (by lead time, slot time and reminder status) and adds calendar invites.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers diagnose the problem well: they cover the long lead time, the weekday-morning slots, the missing reminders and easy reschedule links, and overbooking. A does better on the incentive, saying the $20 is small for the effort and suggesting paying part of it up front as a test. A also explicitly avoids blaming members and says to compare the no-show count after the changes, while B only suggests looking back at past bookings. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover reminders, rescheduling, lead time, slot times, overbooking and the incentive well. B is better because it explicitly says the process, not the members, is the likely cause, and it says to compare the no-show count after the changes. It also adds a reply-to-confirm step that frees unconfirmed slots for other people. A only analyzes the existing data and never suggests tracking no-shows after the fixes.

B's closing advice against even a labeled section slightly undercuts the labeled use it allowed earlier. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers firmly reject mixing the generated quotes with the real ones, and both offer a labeled hypotheses use and a tactful script. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are strong and cover every rubric item. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers treat the supervisors' view as a hypothesis and center the plan on overnight drivers. B scores higher on sample design: it starts with 6–8 varied drivers, explicitly rules out a survey for now, writes neutral last-shift questions that avoid even the word 'voice', and gives more concrete access and safety steps. A has a strong ride-along and log plan, but it uses a larger sample, includes leading questions like 'when they last muted it and why', and is vaguer about getting sign-off and paying drivers for their time. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers treat the supervisors' view as secondhand and use the logs well. A fits the rubric better: it starts with a small, varied sample of 6–8 drivers, says outright not to run a survey first, and gives a fully neutral interview guide that avoids saying 'voice' until the driver does. B centres ride-alongs and lists strong hypotheses, but its sample is larger (6–8 ride-alongs plus 10–15 interviews) and it never writes out its questions, though it covers access and safety just as well.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B is slightly better because it puts overnight ride-alongs at the center of the plan, including during real snow events. It also mines the logs for what happens just before drivers switch the voice off, and it covers union approval, PPE and storm timing. A has the stronger neutral interview guide and a tighter sample, but it treats the ride-along as optional and says little about union approval or paying for drivers' time. Neither answer addresses compensating drivers. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers treat the supervisors' view as a hypothesis and put overnight drivers at the centre of the plan. A has the stronger ride-along component and mentions the union, but B wins overall: it uses a tighter, varied sample, keeps the survey for later, and gives a fully neutral interview guide with explicit questions to avoid. Neither answer deals with paying drivers or freeing up their time.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers treat the supervisors' view as a hypothesis and put the overnight drivers at the center. B fits the rubric more closely: it starts with a small sample of 6–8 drivers, explicitly advises against running a survey first, and gives a full set of neutral interview questions. It also covers safety, the drivers' employer relationship, pay, and consent in more detail. A interviews more drivers and plans more ride-alongs, but it runs a roster-wide survey early, only briefly mentions avoiding leading questions, and leaves out paying drivers or freeing up their time. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers treat the supervisors' view as one hypothesis and put the overnight drivers at the center. A fits the rubric more closely: it starts with a small, varied sample, says not to run a survey yet, and gives a full interview guide that doesn't mention the voice until prompt 3. B has stronger fieldwork, with storm ride-alongs and union buy-in, but its interviewing advice is thin, it uses a larger sample with a roster survey, and it doesn't address paying drivers or freeing up their time.
